title: Crossing the flood
hook: how did you cross? by not halting and not straining (SN 1.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Samyutta Nikaya opened, thousands of short discourses, and your line, gathered by kind. Did you read one? Today we read its very first, and close a week. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

Late at night, a glow fills the Jeta Grove near Savatthi. A deva, a radiant being from the heavens, has come down to see the Buddha. It bows, stands to one side, and asks one question, the question that opens the whole Connected Sayings. How, dear sir, did you cross the flood? The flood, in these texts, is everything that sweeps a person along: wanting, becoming, views, not knowing. The answer is a handful of words in Pali, and it sounds like a riddle. Today: crossing the flood.
screen: `A GLOW IN THE JETA GROVE.` → `HOW DID YOU CROSS THE FLOOD?` → `AN ANSWER LIKE A RIDDLE.`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers: by not halting, friend, and by not straining, I crossed the flood. The deva asks the obvious thing: how? He explains. When I stood still, I sank. When I pushed hard, I was swept away. So, not halting and not straining, I crossed. Take a swimmer in a strong river. Stop moving and you go under. Thrash and fight the current and you wear yourself out and get carried off anyway. What gets you across is steady movement, without either. The Buddhist tradition reads this in many ways. Some commentators say halting means getting stuck in craving and views, and straining means getting carried away by them. Others hear it as the middle way of the very first sermon, between indulgence and harsh effort. Some meditation teachers just hear practical advice: don't quit, don't force. The deva is delighted. It speaks a verse: after a long time, at last, I see a brahmin, a holy one, fully at peace, who without halting, without straining, has crossed over clinging to the world. Then it bows, circles the Buddha, and vanishes. That's the whole discourse. Look back at this week. A warning shouted from a riverbank, the whirlpool ahead. Parents named as first teachers. Effort kept alive, iriyapatha. Word and deed matched, as he speaks, so he does. The short books closed. The Connected Sayings opened, gathered by kind. And now the first of them, back at the water again, with a way across.
screen: `I STOOD STILL AND SANK` · `I PUSHED AND WAS SWEPT AWAY` · `A SWIMMER IN A STRONG RIVER` · `THE DEVA'S VERSE, AND IT VANISHES` · then, large: `NOT HALTING, NOT STRAINING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be a river. Don't stop it, don't push it. When you notice you've drifted off into thoughts, that's halting: gently start moving again by feeling the next breath. When you notice you're gripping, trying hard to breathe well, that's straining: soften the shoulders, the jaw, the belly. Back and forth, finding the place between. Not stuck. Not forcing. Just crossing, one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
Ogha, the flood. The first discourse of the Connected Sayings: the Buddha crossed without halting and without straining, because standing still sinks and pushing gets swept away. Today's word.
Your line: not halting, not straining. Pick one task today you've been either avoiding or forcing, and do ten steady minutes of it, no more, no less. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions describe balanced effort as neither too tight nor too loose, and the first discourse of the Samyutta Nikaya is sometimes cited when they do.

myth: SN 1.1 is the first discourse of the Connected Sayings
the Samyutta Nikaya opens with the deva's question about crossing the flood.
the Buddha says he crossed by trying as hard as he could
he says pushing hard swept him away; he crossed by not halting and not straining.
all Buddhist commentators read halting and straining the same way
some read craving and views, some the middle way, some teachers simply balanced effort.

fork.setup: you're a swimmer in a strong river, trying to reach the far bank. what gets you across, according to SN 1.1?
options: stop and float until the current slows.
fight the current with everything you've got.
keep moving steadily, neither stopping nor straining.
fork.reveal: the Buddha says: when I stood still, I sank; when I pushed, I was swept away. the way across was neither.

original.note: Pali ogha: a flood, the current that sweeps beings along.

trapdoor: what you thought: crossing the flood is about a river journey.
what it means: in SN 1.1, the Buddha crossed the flood of craving and confusion by not halting and not straining.

what a scholar hears: elsewhere the canon names four floods, sensual desire, becoming, views and ignorance; SN 1.1 opens the deva-connected chapter, where heavenly beings question the Buddha in verse.

notes: SN 1.1 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (Jeta Grove, Savatthi, late at night), the Pali appatittham anayuham (not halting, not straining) and the explanation (standing still I sank, striving I was swept away).
Confirm the deva's closing verse paraphrase and that it calls the Buddha a brahmin fully quenched (parinibbuta) who crossed attachment to the world.
The commentarial readings (stuck in craving and views / swept by them; middle way) are summarized loosely.
The four floods (kama, bhava, ditthi, avijja) are from other suttas (e.g. SN 45.171).
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced superlative 'the shortest first chapter of any great book'; 'many teachers' softened to 'some' in teach and myth.
